opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and it's something we've thought about quite a lot. The way I'd frame it is that Genie 3 isn't really a map or a reconstruction engine. It's a world model that has learned a very broad prior about how the world looks and behaves, and then it generates from that. So when you prompt it with something abstract or fantastical, like a floating island, a coral reef city, or some stylized animated world, it's playing to its strengths. There's no single ground truth it has to match, so what you care about is whether it's coherent, whether it's consistent as you move around, and whether the dynamics feel plausible. It tends to do really well there.

With specific real-world locations it's a bit different. If you ask for something iconic, it'll often capture the character of a place quite convincingly: the architecture, the lighting, the general feel of a street in a certain city. But I'd be careful not to overclaim. It isn't guaranteeing geographic accuracy. If you walked down a particular road, you shouldn't expect every building to be exactly where it is in reality. It's generating something that's consistent with what it has learned about that kind of place, rather than retrieving a faithful copy.

So when we assess it, we look at things like visual fidelity, consistency over time, whether the world stays stable when you look away and come back, and how well it follows the prompt. For real places, prompt adherence includes "does this feel like the place?" But we're not treating it as a digital twin. I think that's an important distinction, because for a lot of the uses we're most excited about, like training embodied agents, prototyping, or creative exploration, what matters is diversity and realism of the dynamics, not pixel-perfect reproduction of a real location.

Longer term, grounding these models more tightly in real places is an exciting direction, maybe combining them with other sources of data. But right now I'd say the abstract and imaginative side is where it really shines, and the real-world side is impressive in spirit but shouldn't be mistaken for an accurate replica.

r001.rationale: The response says Genie 3 tends to do well with abstract worlds, while specific real locations may capture a place’s general character but are not geographically accurate replicas.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we spent a lot of time looking at, and it's actually a really interesting distinction. When you think about what the model is doing, it's learned from a huge amount of video data, so it has some sense of what, say, Venice or a mountain range in the Alps looks like in a kind of general, statistical way. If you prompt it with a famous location, you'll often get something that feels right. The canals, the architecture, the lighting all seem plausible, and you can walk around it and it stays consistent, which was the big step for us with Genie 3.

But I'd be careful about the word "specific." It's not a map, it's not geographically accurate, and it's not reproducing a particular street corner from memory. It's generating something that's consistent with the prompt and then committing to that world as you explore it. So if you turned a corner in real Venice you'd see one thing, and in the Genie world you'd see something very Venice-like, but not the actual thing. For our purposes that's fine, and honestly in some ways it's the point. We want environments that an agent can learn in, not a digital twin.

The abstract or imagined worlds are where I think it really shines, because there's no ground truth to be wrong against. You can ask for a floating city made of coral or a cartoon world with strange physics, and the model is free to invent, and it does that in a way that's really coherent over tens of seconds. What matters for us is less photorealism of a known place and more that the world obeys its own rules, that objects persist when you look away and come back, that actions have consistent consequences. Both the real-world-flavoured prompts and the fully abstract ones test that in different ways, and the diversity is what makes it useful as a training ground for agents.

r001.rationale: The response says abstract worlds are where Genie 3 “really shines,” while specific real locations may feel plausible but are not geographically accurate or reproductions of actual places.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s an important distinction between creating a world that looks like a particular place and faithfully reconstructing that place. You might get something that captures the feel of a real-world location, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the streets connect correctly or that everything is where you’d expect it to be. So I’d be cautious about treating it as an accurate representation of somewhere specific.

For imagined or abstract worlds, there’s much more freedom. The question becomes whether the world feels coherent and responds consistently as you move through it, rather than whether it matches a location on a map. Those are different capabilities, and being good at one doesn’t automatically establish the other.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the freedom and coherence goals of abstract worlds with geographic accuracy for real places, but it does not state that Genie 3 matches descriptions of abstract worlds more reliably.
